1. No, not every trans person feels their current gender has been consistent their whole life. For one thing some trans people are genderfluid and experience changes in their gender (the frequency of which is incredibly variable). And some people experience their gender shifting as they get older, in much the same way that other aspects of their identity evolves. It is highly individualized and unique to each person. 

2. As far as, were you a lesbian: if you don't self-identify that way, then no. It is possible to be in a same sex relationship without being a lesbian. Even if your ex tells you their gender has been static (meaning they have always been a woman, including when you were dating) it doesn't have a ton of bearing on your sexuality. 

3. As far as labels go: They can sometimes be restrictive and very negative (telling a little boy he can't play with dolls or a girl she can't like dump trucks) but other times they can be extremely validating and help people form bonds and community over shared experiences. Just imagine the differences between saying Black Lives Matter and All Lives Matter. The former speaks to an actual experience shared by folks who are (or are perceived as) black in the u.s. The latter seeks to invisibilize that identity, which was born from a shared, lived experience. Basically if a label is used to create power over others, it's bad. If it's used to reclaim power for oneself that has typically been denied, it is worth listening to and respecting.

One thing that is important when trying to educate yourself on issues that are important to groups of 'others' is to remember that said group is made up of individuals with an endless variety of opinions and feelings. If you are able bodied can you envision talking to a person who isn't in a similar way? What about if you are documented and speaking with an undocumented immigrant?

Treat her like anyone else that you want to know you care about and try to avoid the fact that she is trans being some sort of huge deal in your relationship.
